new_statements.quote: Le Wɛ est une langue tonale où les tons ont une très grande valeur distinctive, au même titre que les consonnes et les voyelles. Le wɛ a 4 tons simples qui correspondent à 4 registres de hauteur différents: Haut (H), Mi-haut (h), Mi-bas (b), Bas (B). Une syllabe peut ainsi porter un ton simple ou une combinaison de 2 tons. [...] Dans l'ensemble guéré, on trouve ces 13 réalisations, correspondant à 6(+2) tonèmes. En wobè, les 11 réalisations trouvées manifestent 9(+2) tonèmes. Enfin, le nidrou utilise 6(+2) tonèmes correspondant à 8 réalisations. L'indication (+2) représente les tons HB et hB qui ne peuvent apparaître qu'en deuxième syllabe d'un item disyllabique.
new_statements.translation: Wɛ is a tone language in which tones have very high distinctive value, on a par with consonants and vowels. Wɛ has 4 simple tones corresponding to 4 different pitch registers: High (H), Mid-high (h), Mid-low (b), Low (B). A syllable can thus bear a simple tone or a combination of 2 tones. [...] In the Guéré group all 13 realisations are found, corresponding to 6(+2) tonemes. In Wobé the 11 realisations attested represent 9(+2) tonemes. Finally, Nidrou [the Toulepleu variety = Wè Western] uses 6(+2) tonemes corresponding to 8 realisations. '(+2)' stands for the HB and hB tones, which can only occur on the second syllable of a disyllabic item.
new_statements.citation: Bôle-Richard, Rémy. 2006. Unité et diversité du wɛ de Côte d'Ivoire. Journal of West African Languages 33(2): 109-142.

new_statements.rule_in_words: The source characterises Wè (including the Toulepleu/Nidrou variety that is Wè Western) as a four-level register-tone language with lexical contour tones; it describes tonal melodies over mono- and disyllables and consonant-tone interaction, but says nothing at all about word stress or accent — no stress position is stated or denied.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tonal detail only: Nidrou has merged *H and *h, simplified rising tones, and shifts rising components rightward onto the second syllable (rules RN1-RN4, p.140).
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical items in citation form (c. 600 comparative series, mono- and disyllabic nouns/verbs, transcribed phonetically as elicited 1983-1989); no phrase-level prosody discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: Bôle-Richard 2006 is a comparative study of Ivorian Wè; the passage quoted is stated for Wè as a whole and then specifically for 'nidrou', his label for the Toulepleu variety (dialect code N, 2 informants, localité Toulépleu) — this is exactly Glottolog's Wè Western wewe1238 (dialects Nidrou nidr1238, Kaoro kaor1241). Note his caveat (p.115/§1) that 'Nidrou' is also the name of a Wobé-area sous-préfecture near Fakobly (his W3), which is a different lect (Wè Northern, weno1238). The other Wè descriptions in the literature are of Wobé (weno1238: Bearth & Link, Egner, Paradis 1984) or central/southern Guéré (weso1238: Paradis 1983, probably Fisher 1976) or Liberian Western Krahn (west2488: Duitsman, Bing), not of wec.

sources.note: Nothing about stress/accent (the word 'accent' appears only for tone diacritics). Sec. 4 p.125: Wɛ is a tone language with 4 level tones (H, h, b, B) plus rising/falling contours; the Toulepleu 'nidrou' variety (= Wè Western, 2 informants) has 6(+2) tonemes / 8 realisations; sec. 4.2 p.129: nidrou uses 6 tonal contours on monosyllables and 10 on disyllables, derived historically from the Wobé system after devoicing of voiced obstruents.
